title: Bi-Continuous W-Rich Refractory High Entropy Alloy-Cu Composite: Toward Material Innovation of Nuclear Reactor Coolant System.

recollection.starting_material: guess: powders of tungsten, molybdenum, vanadium, tantalum, niobium (forming a W-rich refractory high-entropy alloy) mixed with copper
recollection.intervention: guess: co-sintering or liquid metal dealloying to produce a bi-continuous composite in which the refractory HEA forms one 3-D network and Cu forms the other
recollection.structure: guess: interpenetrating, bi-continuous phases with ~50-50 vol % W-rich HEA matrix and Cu coolant channels, pore/ligament scale 3–10 µm
recollection.mechanism: guess: selective dissolution of Cu from a cast precursor followed by infiltration or coarsening yields interconnected high-entropy alloy ligaments that provide strength while the Cu network supplies high thermal conductivity and coolant pathways
recollection.results: guess: compressive strength >1.2 GPa at 600 °C, thermal conductivity ~150 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, good irradiation resistance predicted; composite shows 2× higher strength than pure Cu and 3× higher thermal conductivity than monolithic refractory HEA, meeting target metrics for advanced reactor coolants

score.note: The recollection tentatively identifies liquid-metal dealloying and the bicontinuous RHEA/Cu networks, but offers incorrect alternatives and misses molten-Cu treatment conditions. Structural details such as the claimed ~50/50 fractions and 3–10 µm scale are wrong, and the actual W-rich interlayer is omitted. The mechanism reverses the key selective-removal process: Ti-rich regions dissolve/exchange into molten Cu rather than Cu being selectively dissolved. The thermal-conductivity estimate of ~150 W m−1 K−1 is near the measured high-temperature value (~140), but most quantitative claims, especially strength and enhancement factors, are unsupported or inaccurate.
